title: Moules à la crème
subtitle: Mussels in white wine and cream
excerpt: Fresh mussels steamed open in white wine, shallots, and butter, finished with a generous pour of cream. The richer, Norman cousin of moules marinières, served with crusty bread or frites.
sourceNotes: Moules à la crème is a Norman preparation of mussels; cream-finished mussels appear in Elizabeth David, French Provincial Cooking (1960) and in the cooking of Normandy and Brittany where both mussels and dairy are plentiful.

content.text: Moules à la crème follows the same method as moules marinières but finishes with cream, which rounds the wine and mussel juices into a sauce rich enough to dip bread into. The cream is added after the mussels have opened and the pan is off the heat; it does not need to cook further.

attrs.title: Buying and preparing mussels
attrs.body: Buy mussels from a fishmonger or a reliable wet fish counter on the day you plan to cook them. They should smell of the sea, not of ammonia. Discard any with broken shells. Before cooking, scrub the shells under cold water and pull out the hairy beard that protrudes from the hinge end. Discard any mussels that remain open after tapping them firmly on the counter.

items.prepNote: scrubbed, beards removed, any open ones discarded

content.text: Melt the butter in a large, deep pot over medium heat. Cook the shallots for 3 minutes until softened. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute more. Add the thyme and bay leaf.

Increase heat to high. Pour in the wine and let it bubble for 1 minute. Add all the mussels at once and clamp the lid on. Cook for 3 to 4 minutes, shaking the pot once or twice, until all the mussels have opened.
Remove from heat. Discard any mussels that have not opened. Pour over the cream and scatter in the chopped parsley. Add a grinding of black pepper. Stir gently to combine.
Ladle into deep bowls and serve immediately with crusty bread to soak up the sauce.

items.symptom: Some mussels have not opened after cooking
items.cause: Dead mussels or not cooked long enough
items.fix: Discard any that remain closed; they are dead. Do not force them. Cook the rest for 1 more minute.

items.cause: The mussels release a lot of liquid
items.fix: Remove the mussels with a slotted spoon and reduce the sauce briefly over high heat before adding the cream.
Mussels need only 3 to 4 minutes. Remove from heat as soon as they open.

items.cause: The mussel liquor is naturally salty
items.fix: Do not add any salt to this dish. Season only with pepper.

content.text: Moules à la crème is Norman cooking: the same mussels as the Breton marinières but finished with the rich cream of Normandy's dairy tradition. The two dishes represent the north of France's two coastal identities. Both are served in the same way: a deep bowl of mussels in their shells with the pot of broth alongside, bread for dipping, and an empty bowl for the shells. This is a recipe that takes 15 minutes from start to table.
